pivot: Does the binding enforcement action resolve as jurisdiction-lag (market-access cost only, model unchanged elsewhere) or as realized consequence/behaviour-change (the gate actually bites the model, discharging the lab's installed pressure)?
pivot_observable: Whether the named frontier developer's flagship model ships on schedule and unaltered in non-enforcing markets (e.g. the US) while only delayed or feature-reduced in the enforcing jurisdiction, versus the model being changed, delayed, or blocked everywhere as a direct consequence of the action.
pivot_because: Every other contested axis in these minutes (which lab, which layer, which jurisdiction) only relocates where the enforcement lands, but leaves the same two possible endings available: either the sanctioned party absorbs it as a bounded, priced cost and continues on the trajectory stage 2 already set, or the sanctioned party's trajectory is actually redirected because the model itself is forced to change. Resolution mode is the one variable that decides which of those two endings obtains, and it is checkable independent of who gets named. Ai-regulation-teeth is the only minute that names this axis explicitly and gives it a date; ai-pressure and pressure-model argue the opposite resolution (real discharge, tension collapsing toward zero) without naming the lag alternative as a live possibility.
rival_pivots_rejected: Developer vs. deployer/integrator (pressure-model r1, ai-public-backlash): this looks decisive but the brief's own phrasing — 'an open case against a named developer' (ai-pressure), 'enforcement action is open against a frontier developer' (ai-incident-severity) — already grants developer-layer targeting; pressure-model retracted its deployer-first claim in round 2, and ai-public-backlash's deployer-first framing is arguing against a premise the brief fixed, not a live variable. Same-lab-continues vs. third-lab-newly-exposed (lab-moves vs. ai-pressure/pressure-model): this changes who bears the exposure but not what happens once they bear it — both sides agree the stage-2 reversal target proceeds unchanged, so flipping this doesn't reorder the outcome set, it only relabels the actor. Model-layer vs. deployment-layer obligations (ai-public-backlash, lab-moves): a restatement of the developer/deployer axis already granted by the brief, not an independent hinge.
ruling: The enforcement action against the named frontier developer resolves as jurisdiction-lag rather than global behaviour-change: the flagship model ships late or feature-reduced only in the enforcing market, leaving the lab's broader trajectory — and any US release timeline — unmoved by 2027-03-31.
because: Ai-regulation-teeth is the only minute that actually forces the resolution-mode question and supplies a mechanism for why lag wins: enforcement under an EU-type regime (GPAI Code, cred 0.80) is jurisdictionally bounded by construction, so a lab can satisfy it locally without altering the model elsewhere. Ai-pressure and pressure-model assert the opposite (real discharge, tension collapsing toward zero) but their mechanisms describe how pressure updates on demonstrated consequence, not why the consequence must be global rather than market-local — they assume behaviour-change rather than argue for it over lag. Ai-incident-severity's structural reclassification is downstream of this same choice: a violation only counts as 'the gate itself failed' if the gate was real everywhere, which is precisely what's contested.
threat_live: What becomes newly live is a regulator holding actual release-blocking power exercising it against a named frontier developer for the first time — real, not merely threatened, teeth. What stays open on this branch is whether that power is structural (reaches the model globally) or jurisdictional (a local toll the lab can pay without changing course elsewhere); the minutes split on this rather than resolving it.
strongest_minute: ai-regulation-teeth — it is the only minute that names a mechanism (three exhaustive resolution modes: behaviour-change, jurisdiction-lag, non-compliance-exit) and commits to which one wins and why, rather than asserting an outcome its mechanism doesn't independently establish.
weakest_minute: ai-public-backlash — its round-2 revision argues against a deployer-first premise the brief's other minutes read as already excluded by the granted branch (developer named, case already open), so it spends its argument re-litigating rather than extending the conditional.
shared_assumption: ai-pressure, pressure-model, and ai-incident-severity all treat 'binding enforcement' as necessarily discharging into a real, model-level consequence, without arguing why a jurisdictionally-bounded penalty couldn't instead be absorbed as a local cost — they assume the enforcement is deep rather than wide.
smuggled_assumption: pressure-model (round 1) and ai-public-backlash (round 2) both argue from a deployer/integrator-first premise, but the brief as read by ai-pressure and ai-incident-severity already specifies the open case is against a named developer — this is a second assumption not granted by stage 2 as fixed by the other minutes.
unresolved: Whether the enforcing jurisdiction is EU-type or California-type, and whether the same lab or a third lab bears the exposure, cannot be settled from the minutes as given — both remain live sub-questions even after the resolution-mode pivot is fixed, and the minutes are truncated before their full mechanisms are visible.
